package_info.package_manager: Windows DLL (malicious loader, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (malware loader, not versioned in the traditional sense)
package_info.why_malicious: PowGoop is a malicious loader DLL that impersonates the legitimate Google Update component (GoogleUpdate.dll) to evade detection. It is deployed by the MuddyWater APT group to deliver the Thanos ransomware, which can also function as a wiper, to targeted systems. The loader's primary function is to decrypt and execute additional malicious payloads in memory, making the entire DLL inherently malicious and a critical part of the attack chain.

execution_context.trigger: When the DLL is loaded by a process expecting GoogleUpdate.dll (e.g., via DLL hijacking or direct loading)
execution_context.file_location: C:\Program Files\Google\Update\GoogleUpdate.dll (or similar path, masquerading as legitimate DLL)
required_permissions: process execution (create new process or inject code)
memory access (allocate and write memory for payload execution)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the DLL is loaded by a process expecting GoogleUpdate.dll, the exported function (e.g., DllRegisterServer) decrypts an embedded payload using a custom routine, allocates memory, writes the decrypted payload into memory, and executes it in the context of the host process, resulting in the in-memory deployment of the Thanos ransomware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The DLL is named and located to mimic a legitimate Google Update component but contains code that decrypts and executes an embedded payload in memory, a hallmark of malware loaders. The use of in-memory execution and custom decryption routines is designed to evade static detection and analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate Google Update DLL should only perform update-related operations and never decrypt or execute arbitrary code in memory. The presence of code that loads and runs an encrypted payload is inconsistent with any expected behavior for this DLL.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate updaters may use encrypted payloads for self-updating, but they do not execute arbitrary code in memory via exported functions, nor do they masquerade as system DLLs in non-standard locations.
key_indicators: DLL named GoogleUpdate.dll located outside standard update directories
Exported functions (e.g., DllRegisterServer) that decrypt and execute code in memory
Absence of legitimate update logic or Google Update functionality
Presence of embedded encrypted payloads within the DLL binary

execution_context.trigger: After the loader executes the decrypted payload in memory (post-loader execution)
execution_context.file_location: In-memory payload delivered by PowGoop (Thanos ransomware binary, not written to disk)
required_permissions: process termination (kill processes to unlock files)
system modification (overwrite MBR or critical system files)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After being executed in memory by the loader, the ransomware enumerates files in target directories, encrypts each file not on a whitelist, deletes the original files, writes a ransom note to affected directories, and may optionally overwrite the Master Boot Record (MBR) or critical system files, resulting in data loss, ransom demand, or system inoperability.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs mass file encryption and deletion, writes ransom notes, and can overwrite the system's MBR or critical files, all of which are definitive behaviors of ransomware and wiper malware. These actions are destructive and intended to extort or permanently damage the victim.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate software should encrypt user files en masse, delete originals, write ransom notes, or overwrite the system's boot record without explicit, informed user consent. Such actions are fundamentally malicious.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or archival software may encrypt files, but they do not delete originals, write ransom notes, or modify the MBR. Legitimate disk utilities that modify the MBR do so only with explicit user authorization and never in conjunction with file encryption and ransom demands.
key_indicators: Mass file encryption and deletion in user and system directories
Creation of ransom notes (e.g., README.txt, HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt) in affected folders
Overwriting or wiping of the Master Boot Record (MBR) or other critical system files
Network activity to command-and-control servers following encryption

attack_chain.action: The PowGoop loader DLL is delivered to the target system, masquerading as a legitimate Google Update DLL (GoogleUpdate.dll) and placed in a directory where it will be loaded by a legitimate process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the loader by a legitimate process, typically via DLL hijacking or search order manipulation

attack_chain.action: The loader DLL is executed by the legitimate process, triggering its exported function, which decrypts and executes the embedded Thanos ransomware payload in memory.
attack_chain.leads_to: In-memory execution of the ransomware payload without writing it to disk

attack_chain.action: The Thanos ransomware payload, now running in memory, enumerates and encrypts files, deletes originals, writes ransom notes, and may overwrite the MBR or critical files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data loss, ransom demand, or system inoperability (final objective of the attack)

behavioral_signatures: DLLs named after legitimate system or update components (e.g., GoogleUpdate.dll) appearing in non-standard or unexpected directories
DLLs exporting functions that decrypt and execute embedded payloads in memory upon being loaded
Processes loading DLLs with no legitimate update logic but containing custom decryption and in-memory execution routines
Mass file encryption and deletion activity across user and system directories
Creation of ransom notes (e.g., README.txt, HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt) in multiple directories
Attempts to overwrite or wipe the Master Boot Record (MBR) or other critical system files
file_indicators: Presence of GoogleUpdate.dll in directories not associated with legitimate Google software (e.g., application folders, user directories)
DLLs with embedded encrypted payloads (high entropy sections within the binary)
Ransom notes such as README.txt or HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt appearing in user directories
Absence of legitimate Google Update metadata or digital signatures in the DLL
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known or suspected command-and-control (C2) infrastructure following DLL load events (may use HTTP/S, DNS tunneling, or cloud services)
Beaconing or exfiltration attempts initiated by processes that have loaded suspicious GoogleUpdate.dll files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for DLLs named GoogleUpdate.dll appearing in non-standard locations or loaded by processes unrelated to Google software. Analyze DLL exports for functions that decrypt and execute in-memory payloads. Flag processes that perform mass file encryption and deletion, create ransom notes, or attempt to overwrite the MBR. Correlate these events with suspicious outbound network activity, especially following the loading of suspect DLLs. Use high-entropy analysis to identify embedded encrypted payloads within DLLs and verify digital signatures to distinguish legitimate from malicious files.
